cells.tense: You are the one already reading the ground and handing people the next step.
cells.ask: Before a decision that's already moving, write the one sentence that says what you can currently see, read it once, then go ahead with it anyway.
cells.core:
The fog hasn't stopped you. You've got a read on what's actually going on — where the confusion really sits, what move cuts through it without making anyone pretend they understand — and you hand that read to people as a next step rather than a speech.

What's good here is that you trust small light over false daylight. You don't wait for the whole road to appear before anyone moves. People around you stop hunting for certainty and start standing on the ground they're actually on. The line to hold is that the way you guide gets built on real thinking about real things, not on whatever's loudest or nearest. When that holds, the direction you give carries. If you skip the next step, nothing goes wrong. You just don't build what was next.
cells.sheetLine: You don't wait for the whole road. You hand people the next step.
cells.verb: charting a way through fog for people who can't see it yet
cells.place: a place where the next step is visible and the road after it isn't

cells.tense: You are going to keep steering until every person in the room is out of water they are not in.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you are not currently responsible for, leave it alone for a day, and tell whoever is actually holding it that it's theirs.
cells.core:
You're already running the whole crossing in your head. Someone hasn't asked yet and you've decided how to get them through — where the trouble will be, which turn is safe, what they'll need from you by the time they arrive. Anticipation is a real skill. When it runs ahead of what's here, it starts steering things nobody handed you the wheel for.

What's good in this is that you can do the patient work of getting people across, and the people around you trust that. The step back exists so the work you do stays work that's actually yours. Letting a thing be somebody else's is not abandoning them; the discipline here is finishing one crossing before you launch the next. When you hold that line, the room settles instead of straining against you.

cells.tense: You knew the water and you have stopped handing anyone the read you carry.
cells.ask: Take one small decision now happening around you, say the single next step out loud to one person there, then let the conversation take it from there.
cells.core:
You knew the way through this part. The reading of the ground hasn't moved; the offering went quiet. Maybe the room was already too bright, or nobody was asking, or being the one who says it out loud stopped feeling worth the trouble. So you waited to be asked. The waiting can outlast the reason for it.

What's good in this is that you can sit inside uncertainty without needing it solved first, which is exactly what leading through continuous fog requires. What has starved is the private sense of what's fair to say out loud, and to whom. Feeding that back in isn't about forcing feeling or pushing effort. It's putting one honest read in front of one person and letting the exchange do what it does. Whatever returns is information, not a verdict.

cells.tense: You are already standing where the next step gets decided and you describe it as if it decided itself.
cells.ask: On one piece of work that has been moving without you saying so, put your name on it once — to yourself first, then to one person in it with you.
cells.core:
Look at a room where people gather before something begins — the spot they come to when they don't know what to do next. Something is already convening them, and in your account that thing is just what happened. It isn't. People in that room are turning toward you for the read, not toward the schedule, and you keep calling that coincidence or calling it adults handling themselves.

What's good here is that you can navigate the middle of something without needing the outline, and when two people are walking the same unknown and you say so, it goes further than either could alone. The step below this is smaller than you think: name one connection that has been forming without you claiming it, then start from where it actually is. That's not about credit. It's about the thing going where it's going with both hands on it.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is currently navigating ambiguity or that their uncertainty has a discernible shape the reading can name; the record gives the seat, not their life. A reader could object that nothing here is actually in question for them right now, or that what looks like leading in fog is only a schedule they keep. The ask survives being wrong because it produces a real effect on someone — a finish line said out loud moves the line whether or not the read is right. The sentence that serves the writer rather than the person would be anything like 'you're the one who can see the way through' — it flatters the seat instead of naming what it is doing.
